questions.question: A user receives an email appearing to be from their bank, urging them to click a link and verify their account details. The link leads to a convincing replica of the bank's website hosted on an unfamiliar domain. What type of attack is this?
options: Vishing — a voice-based attack in which a caller impersonates a trusted institution to extract sensitive information
Pretexting — fabricating a detailed backstory to build trust and manipulate a target into revealing confidential data
Smishing — a text-message lure that directs the recipient to a malicious link or prompts a call to a spoofed number
Phishing — an email-based attack using a spoofed sender and a counterfeit site to harvest user credentials
questions.explanation: Phishing uses deceptive emails with spoofed senders and lookalike websites to trick users into entering credentials on attacker-controlled pages. Vishing and smishing are closely related social-engineering variants but use voice calls and SMS as the delivery channel, not email.

questions.question: A forensic team investigates a financial database and finds that a privileged account was used to manipulate stored interest-rate calculations over a 6-week period. All authorized users retained read access throughout, and no data was exfiltrated. Which element of the CIA triad was MOST directly violated?
options: Availability — authorized personnel were periodically denied access to the affected records during each manipulation event
Confidentiality — the privileged account accessed data beyond its authorized classification boundary
Non-repudiation — the audit log did not record the account name associated with each transaction
Integrity — stored values were altered without authorization, compromising data accuracy
questions.explanation: Integrity ensures data remains accurate and unmodified; unauthorized alteration of stored financial calculations is a direct integrity violation regardless of whether data was disclosed. Availability was unaffected because users retained read access throughout, and confidentiality was unaffected because no data left the system.

questions.question: A company's remote-access policy requires employees to enter their password and then approve a push notification on their registered smartphone before VPN access is granted. The smartphone must be physically present for the login to succeed. Which authentication concept does this implement?
options: Multi-factor authentication, combining a knowledge factor and a possession factor from distinct categories
Single sign-on (SSO), allowing a single credential set to authenticate the user across multiple systems
Step-up authentication, which re-prompts the same credential type when a session attempts privileged actions
Federated identity, which delegates authentication to a trusted third-party identity provider across boundaries
questions.explanation: Multi-factor authentication requires factors from at least two different categories — here, 'something you know' (password) and 'something you have' (smartphone). SSO simplifies access by using one set of credentials for multiple systems, which is the opposite of adding a second distinct factor.

questions.question: A penetration tester on the same open Wi-Fi network as a target uses ARP spoofing to redirect the target's traffic through the tester's laptop before forwarding it to the hotel gateway, capturing session cookies in transit. Which class of attack does this scenario describe?
options: Replay attack — re-submitting captured authentication tokens to impersonate the original user after the session ends
Man-in-the-middle attack — covertly inserting between two parties to observe or alter their communications undetected
Denial-of-service attack — flooding gateway resources with spoofed packets to prevent other guests from connecting
Credential stuffing — cycling through a leaked username-password list against the hotel portal's authentication endpoint
questions.explanation: ARP spoofing lets the attacker silently relay traffic between the victim and the gateway while reading or modifying it — the defining characteristic of a man-in-the-middle attack. A replay attack reuses previously captured tokens after a session ends; it does not involve real-time interception and relay of live traffic.

questions.question: A network architect must enforce traffic policy between the corporate LAN and the internet, blocking connections to disallowed ports and permitting only approved protocols. The solution should track TCP session state and apply rules based on packet headers at the network perimeter. Which technology best satisfies this requirement?
options: Stateful firewall, which tracks TCP session state and enforces port and protocol rules at the network boundary
Network IDS, which passively mirrors traffic and generates alerts without intercepting or blocking any packets
Web application firewall (WAF), which inspects HTTP/HTTPS payloads at Layer 7 to block web-specific exploits
Reverse proxy, which relays client requests through an intermediary and can cache responses from origin servers
questions.explanation: A stateful firewall maintains a connection-state table for TCP sessions and enforces allow/deny rules based on IP address, port, and protocol — exactly what is needed for perimeter enforcement between LAN and internet. A WAF operates only on HTTP/HTTPS at Layer 7 and is designed to block web application exploits, not general port-and-protocol filtering.

questions.question: A hospital's file servers become inaccessible over a holiday weekend. Administrators discover every patient-record folder has been encrypted, and a ransom note demands 10 Bitcoin in exchange for the decryption key. Security logs show the encryption was performed by a remote process that spread through a compromised service account. What category of malware caused this incident?
options: Worm, which self-replicates across network shares by exploiting service vulnerabilities without human interaction
Spyware, which covertly captures user activity and transmits harvested credentials to a remote collection server
Ransomware, which encrypts victim files and withholds the decryption key pending payment of a demanded ransom
Rootkit, which embeds itself in the OS kernel to maintain persistent privileged access while hiding its presence
questions.explanation: Ransomware encrypts data and withholds the key until a ransom is paid — the Bitcoin demand and encrypted patient records are defining indicators. A worm also propagates through a network autonomously, but its goal is self-replication and spread, not file encryption for extortion.

questions.question: What does PKI stand for and what does it provide?
options: Private Key Infrastructure — a system storing symmetric keys in hardware appliances for enterprise encryption
Protocol Key Interface — a network layer standard enabling encrypted tunnels between routers and switches
Public Key Infrastructure — a framework for managing digital certificates and public-key encryption
Public Knowledge Interface — a federated repository sharing vulnerability data and threat intelligence feeds
questions.explanation: PKI is a framework of policies, hardware, software, and procedures for creating, distributing, managing, and revoking digital certificates. It enables secure communications and identity verification.

questions.question: A financial application encrypts gigabytes of transaction logs at rest and uses TLS to protect connections between its app server and clients over the public internet. During a code review a developer asks why two different encryption methods are required. Which statement correctly explains the design choice?
options: Symmetric algorithms (e.g., AES) encrypt bulk data efficiently with a shared key; asymmetric algorithms (e.g., RSA/ECDH) negotiate that shared key across the untrusted channel
Asymmetric algorithms handle bulk data with lower CPU overhead than symmetric; symmetric encryption is reserved for verifying digital signatures during the TLS handshake only
Both algorithm types require a pre-shared key established out-of-band; the distinction is driven entirely by key length, not by performance or operational use-case differences
Symmetric encryption cannot protect data at rest and is limited to in-transit traffic, so asymmetric algorithms handle storage while symmetric is used solely for the TLS handshake
questions.explanation: Symmetric encryption (e.g., AES) uses the same key for both encryption and decryption, making it highly efficient for large data volumes such as transaction logs stored at rest. Asymmetric encryption (e.g., RSA, ECDH) uses a key pair so that two parties can securely agree on a shared session key without ever transmitting it — this is why TLS uses asymmetric for the handshake and symmetric for bulk data transfer. Option B is incorrect because asymmetric algorithms are orders of magnitude slower than symmetric and are never used for bulk data encryption.

questions.question: Threat intelligence analysts discover that attackers are actively exploiting a remote-code-execution flaw in a widely deployed enterprise VPN appliance. The vendor has not yet acknowledged the vulnerability, no CVE identifier has been assigned, and no mitigation guidance is available. How should this vulnerability be classified?
options: Critical CVE — a flaw formally registered in the NVD with a CVSS score calculated and published by NIST
End-of-life vulnerability — a flaw that persists because the affected version no longer receives vendor patches
Zero-day vulnerability — actively exploited before the vendor is aware and while no patch or fix exists
N-day vulnerability — a disclosed flaw for which a vendor patch exists but has not been widely deployed
questions.explanation: A zero-day vulnerability is exploited in the wild before the vendor knows about it and before any patch or official mitigation is available — the absence of a CVE, no vendor acknowledgment, and active exploitation are the key indicators. An n-day differs because the vendor has already disclosed the vulnerability and a patch exists, even if many deployments remain unpatched.

questions.question: What is the purpose of an IDS (Intrusion Detection System)?
options: Block and filter malicious network packets inline in real time by sitting between network segments
Monitor and alert on suspicious activity or policy violations without blocking traffic
Automate patch deployment across endpoints to close vulnerabilities before attackers can exploit them
Provide centralized log aggregation and correlation of security events across the enterprise environment
questions.explanation: An IDS monitors network traffic or host activity and alerts administrators to suspicious behavior. Unlike an IPS (Intrusion Prevention System), an IDS does not actively block threats.

questions.question: A PKI engineer is tasked with updating the organization's internal certificate authority to align with current NIST cryptographic transition requirements. The existing CA signs certificate requests using SHA-1. Which algorithm should replace SHA-1 for all new signing operations?
options: MD5 — 128-bit output, widely supported and computationally efficient for bulk certificate issuance
SHA-1 — 160-bit output, still accepted by many legacy CAs for internal non-public certificate chains
SHA-256 — current NIST standard for new digital signatures; approved for all PKI signing operations
BLAKE2b — faster than SHA-256 with equivalent output size, but absent from the NIST approved list for PKI use
questions.explanation: NIST deprecated SHA-1 for digital signature generation and mandates SHA-256 or stronger (SHA-2/SHA-3 family) for new certificate signing operations. MD5 was deprecated even earlier due to demonstrated collision vulnerabilities. BLAKE2b is cryptographically strong but is not included in NIST SP 800-131A's approved algorithm list for PKI signing, making it unsuitable for a compliance-aligned CA.

questions.question: A threat actor calls an organization's IT help desk, claims to be the newly hired CFO, and says they forgot their VPN credentials while traveling. The help desk agent resets the account without verifying identity. Which attack category BEST describes the technique the threat actor used?
options: Social engineering — manipulating people through deception rather than technical exploits
Replay attack — reusing previously captured authentication tokens to authenticate as a known user
Credential stuffing — systematically submitting leaked username-password pairs against the portal
Pass-the-hash — authenticating with a stolen NTLM credential hash to bypass password requirements
questions.explanation: Social engineering exploits human trust and authority rather than software vulnerabilities — the attacker achieved their goal through impersonation alone, never touching a technical control. Replay attacks, credential stuffing, and pass-the-hash are all technical exploitation methods that require captured tokens or credential data; none involves the psychological manipulation used here.

questions.question: A financial institution runs firewalls, IDS sensors, endpoint agents, and authentication servers that each produce independent logs. Analysts frequently miss multi-step attacks because relevant data is scattered across disconnected systems. Management wants a single platform to centralize security telemetry, identify threats that span multiple sources, and generate prioritized alerts. Which technology category addresses this requirement?
options: SOAR — executes automated playbooks to handle enrichment, cross-tool response actions, and ticket closure without requiring manual analyst intervention per alert
CASB — intercepts user traffic to cloud services to enforce data governance, detect anomalous uploads, and discover unsanctioned shadow-IT applications
SIEM — aggregates log data from across the environment, applies correlation rules to detect multi-source threats, and generates prioritized alerts for analysts
NDR — passively analyzes network flow metadata and packet contents to detect lateral movement and encrypted C2 channels that host-based sensors may independently miss
questions.explanation: A SIEM centralizes log collection from every security data source, normalizes the data into a common format, and applies correlation rules to surface attack sequences that no single system would reveal alone. A SOAR platform automates responses to existing alerts but does not aggregate logs or perform cross-source detection — it consumes SIEM output rather than replacing it.

questions.question: What is a DDoS (Distributed Denial of Service) attack?
options: Exfiltrating sensitive records from multiple organizations simultaneously through a coordinated espionage campaign
Overwhelming a target with traffic from many distributed sources, making it unavailable to legitimate users
Gaining unauthorized access to multiple servers by exploiting a single flaw in a widely shared software library
Coordinating simultaneous physical intrusions against multiple data center locations to destroy hardware assets
questions.explanation: DDoS uses thousands of compromised machines (botnet) to flood a target with traffic or requests, exhausting resources and preventing legitimate access. Mitigated by scrubbing centers and rate limiting.

questions.question: After a breach, forensics reveals that attackers moved from the DMZ to the internal finance subnet in under 10 minutes. A single perimeter firewall with a misconfigured allow-all rule for east-west traffic was the only control between segments — no IDS, no endpoint detection, no logging. The CISO demands a full architecture redesign. Which security principle should govern the new design?
options: Least privilege — restrict every service account and process to the minimum permissions required for its function
Defense in depth — apply multiple overlapping controls (segmentation, IDS, endpoint detection) so one misconfigured layer cannot grant unrestricted access
Security by obscurity — remove internal subnet details from documentation and contractor diagrams to reduce attacker reconnaissance value
Zero trust — mandate continuous cryptographic verification of every east-west connection, eliminating implicit trust within the data center perimeter boundary
questions.explanation: Defense in depth directly addresses the root cause: the architecture relied on a single control that failed. Layering segmentation, IDS/IPS, endpoint detection, and logging means no single misconfiguration gives unrestricted lateral access. Zero trust (option D) is a related but distinct strategy focused on per-session authentication and access control; it does not by itself add the detection and containment layers that would have slowed the attacker in this scenario.

questions.question: What is a SQL injection attack?
options: Uploading executable malware into a database server's file system via a misconfigured MSSQL service account
Performing a brute-force credential attack against a database server login page using automated tooling
Intercepting unencrypted database backup files transmitted over the network to extract sensitive records
Inserting malicious SQL code into an application input field to manipulate the database
questions.explanation: SQL injection exploits poor input validation to inject malicious SQL statements, potentially allowing an attacker to read/modify data, bypass authentication, or execute OS commands.

questions.question: What is the purpose of security awareness training?
options: Reduce human error by educating employees about security threats, policies, and best practices
Train development staff to write secure code using OWASP guidelines embedded in the software delivery pipeline
Configure and tune security tooling so analysts receive fewer false positives and respond to real alerts faster
Replace technical controls like MFA with behavioral change programs that modify how users interact with systems
questions.explanation: Security awareness training addresses the human element — the most common attack vector. It helps employees recognize phishing, use strong passwords, handle data properly, and follow security policies.

questions.question: What is a vulnerability assessment vs a penetration test?
options: Vulnerability assessments and penetration tests are interchangeable; both are delivered using the same automated toolset
Vulnerability assessment identifies weaknesses; penetration test actively exploits them to determine real-world impact
Penetration tests are fully automated Nessus scans; vulnerability assessments always involve a human tester manually probing
Vulnerability assessments require written vendor approval, whereas penetration tests need no authorization to proceed
questions.explanation: Vulnerability assessment scans and identifies potential weaknesses. Penetration testing goes further — it attempts to actively exploit vulnerabilities to demonstrate real impact, simulating an attacker.

questions.question: What does AAA stand for in network security?
options: Antivirus, Authentication, Authorization
Access, Audit, Administration
Authentication, Authorization, Accounting
Application, API, Authentication
questions.explanation: AAA: Authentication (verify identity), Authorization (determine what access is permitted), Accounting (log what the user did). RADIUS and TACACS+ are common AAA protocols.

questions.question: What is data loss prevention (DLP)?
options: Software that automatically backs up user files to an offsite cloud repository on a scheduled recovery cycle
A database encryption solution that protects stored records by applying AES-256 to all sensitive fields at rest
A user activity monitor that alerts managers when employees access files outside of their normal working hours
Technology that detects and prevents unauthorized transmission of sensitive data outside the organization
questions.explanation: DLP solutions monitor and control data movement (email, USB, cloud uploads) to prevent sensitive information (PII, financial data, IP) from leaving the organization without authorization.

questions.question: A security researcher analyzes a crash dump from a legacy C-based file parsing library. The debugger shows the instruction pointer holds a value sourced directly from the user-supplied test file, and adjacent fields on the stack frame contain bytes from the parsed input. ASLR and stack canaries were both disabled. Which vulnerability class BEST describes the root cause?
options: Integer overflow — arithmetic wraps past the integer type's maximum value, silently corrupting adjacent data structures
Buffer overflow — input data exceeds the allocated buffer's bounds, overwriting adjacent memory and altering control flow
Format string vulnerability — attacker-controlled printf specifiers expose or overwrite arbitrary memory locations
Use-after-free — freed heap memory is accessed via a dangling pointer after reallocation, letting attackers influence object contents
questions.explanation: A buffer overflow occurs when a write operation exceeds the bounds of its allocated buffer, overwriting adjacent memory — in this scenario, bytes from the input file overwrote the stack frame and redirected the instruction pointer. Integer overflows are a distinct arithmetic class that can sometimes precede buffer overflows but are a different root cause. Format string vulnerabilities exploit printf-family format specifiers, not buffer bounds. Use-after-free involves accessing freed heap memory, a separate memory-safety class from stack-based buffer overflows.

questions.question: A development team's penetration test report flagged two critical findings: a query parameter that passes unsanitized input directly to a SQL statement, and an admin login page with no brute-force rate limiting. The team wants a single authoritative reference to categorize both findings and guide prioritization of remediation across their web application. Which resource should they consult?
options: NIST SP 800-53 — a comprehensive catalog of security and privacy controls mapped to federal impact levels and FISMA requirements
CIS Critical Security Controls — 18 prioritized safeguards targeting enterprise-wide defensive posture against common attack techniques
OWASP Top 10 — ranks the ten most critical web application risk categories and provides developer-focused remediation guidance
OWASP ASVS — a tiered requirements checklist for designing and verifying security across the web application development lifecycle
questions.explanation: The OWASP Top 10 is the standard reference for categorizing web application risks — SQL injection and broken authentication (lack of brute-force protection) are both named risk categories in the list. NIST SP 800-53 provides broad enterprise security controls, not web-app risk rankings. CIS Controls target enterprise-wide defensive posture rather than per-vulnerability web risk prioritization. OWASP ASVS is a verification standard for application design and testing, not a risk-ranking reference for triaging discovered findings.

questions.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
options: Authentication and authorization are synonymous terms describing the process of verifying user identity for access
Authorization happens before authentication in modern zero-trust systems — permissions are evaluated before identity
Authentication: verifying WHO you are (identity). Authorization: determining WHAT you are allowed to do (permissions)
Authentication generates an access token that simultaneously proves identity and grants specific resource permissions
questions.explanation: AuthN (authentication) = proving identity (password, fingerprint, certificate). AuthZ (authorization) = what actions/resources are permitted after authentication. Both are required for access control.

questions.question: What is a honeypot in cybersecurity?
options: An encrypted password vault that stores service account credentials and rotates them automatically on a schedule
A firewall rule category that redirects suspicious traffic to a quarantine VLAN for automated sandbox analysis
A VPN endpoint that tunnels traffic from remote workers securely into the corporate network perimeter
A decoy system designed to attract, detect, and study attackers by appearing to be a legitimate vulnerable target
questions.explanation: Honeypots are deliberately vulnerable fake systems that detect and analyze attacks. When an attacker interacts with a honeypot, it triggers alerts and captures attack techniques.

questions.question: A security team discovers a missing authentication check on an internal admin portal. A nation-state group known to target the industry is actively scanning for such portals. The CISO asks for a risk statement using standard risk-model vocabulary. Which mapping is correct?
options: Missing auth check = vulnerability; nation-state group = threat; their combined exposure = risk
Missing auth check = threat; nation-state group = vulnerability; admin portal = risk
Nation-state group = risk; missing auth check = threat; the admin portal = vulnerability
Risk is measured by patch age only; threats and vulnerabilities are qualitative assessments only
questions.explanation: In the standard risk model, a vulnerability is a system weakness (the missing auth check), a threat is an actor or event capable of exploiting it (the nation-state group), and risk is the resulting exposure — typically quantified as likelihood × impact. Options B and C swap the definitions of threat and vulnerability, which would invert risk prioritization and lead to hardening the threat actor rather than patching the exploitable weakness.

questions.question: What is a certificate revocation list (CRL)?
options: A browser-maintained registry listing certificate authorities that have exceeded their annual issuance quota
A list published by a CA of certificates that have been revoked before their expiration date (due to key compromise, etc.)
A database of SSL certificates that expired naturally through their scheduled validity period without early revocation
A signed OCSP response cache that pre-validates TLS certificates on behalf of clients to reduce handshake latency
questions.explanation: CRLs are published by Certificate Authorities listing revoked certificates by serial number. OCSP (Online Certificate Status Protocol) is a more efficient real-time alternative to CRL checking.

questions.question: A forensics team obtains a multi-year archive of a company's TLS-encrypted traffic and legally acquires the web server's long-term private key. They discover the archived sessions still cannot be decrypted. Which TLS feature explains this outcome?
options: Certificate pinning — the client hardcodes the expected server certificate fingerprint and rejects any substitute key
Perfect forward secrecy — session keys are ephemeral and cannot be recovered from the server's long-term private key
HSTS preloading — the browser enforced HTTPS connections but this policy does not protect past recorded sessions
OCSP stapling — the CA validates certificate revocation status in real time but does not affect session key recoverability
questions.explanation: Perfect forward secrecy (PFS) uses ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange (ECDHE) to derive a unique session key that is discarded immediately after the session ends — even possessing the server's long-term private key cannot reconstruct it, so archived ciphertext is permanently unreadable. Certificate pinning, HSTS, and OCSP stapling are valuable TLS controls but none of them affect whether historical session keys can be recovered after the fact.

questions.question: An IAM team manages access for 2,000 employees by defining named job-function profiles — Analyst, Developer, Manager — and attaching permissions to those profiles. A new hire receives access automatically by being added to the appropriate profile. Which access control model does this describe?
options: RBAC — users are assigned to named roles and inherit that role's permissions without individual grants
MAC — the OS enforces classification labels and clearance levels regardless of resource owner intent
DAC — individual resource owners decide who can access their own files, shares, or database records
ABAC — access decisions evaluate multiple attributes including user department, device posture, and time of day
questions.explanation: RBAC centralizes permissions in job-function roles rather than individuals — a new Analyst inherits exactly the Analyst role's permissions with no per-user grants needed. MAC relies on OS-enforced security labels; DAC lets owners control their own resource permissions directly; ABAC evaluates dynamic attribute combinations per request — all three differ fundamentally from the role-inheritance model described in the scenario.

questions.question: What is cross-site scripting (XSS)?
options: Injecting malicious client-side scripts into web pages viewed by other users — allows cookie theft, session hijacking, and redirects
Executing scripts across multiple compromised servers to aggregate compute resources for a distributed mining operation
Injecting forged server-side requests that exploit implicit trust between a web server and its internal backend APIs
Inserting specially crafted SQL statements through web form inputs to retrieve or modify records from a database
questions.explanation: XSS injects malicious JavaScript into web pages. Stored XSS: saved in database, runs for all users. Reflected XSS: in URL parameters. DOM XSS: manipulates client-side DOM. Prevention: output encoding, CSP.

questions.question: What is a VPN and what encryption protocols does it use?
options: A forward proxy server that caches web content and filters outbound URLs by category and reputation score
Virtual Private Network — encrypts traffic between endpoints over untrusted networks. Protocols: IPSec, SSL/TLS, OpenVPN, WireGuard
A stateful packet inspection firewall deployed at the network perimeter to block threats and log all connections
An SD-WAN overlay that routes inter-datacenter traffic across MPLS circuits with QoS prioritization policies
questions.explanation: VPNs create encrypted tunnels protecting data in transit. Site-to-site VPN: connects offices over internet. Remote access VPN: connects users. Common protocols: IPSec/IKEv2, OpenVPN (TLS), WireGuard (modern, fast).

questions.question: A security firm is hired to evaluate a regional bank's external attack surface under a signed statement of work. The team begins by collecting publicly available information about the bank's infrastructure and personnel from open sources. They then actively probe discovered hosts, gain access through an identified service vulnerability, pivot to an internal server, and deliver a written report with prioritized remediation recommendations. Which engagement model does this describe?
options: Vulnerability assessment — automated scanning that identifies and ranks weaknesses without any active exploitation of discovered hosts
Penetration test — a structured authorized engagement covering reconnaissance, exploitation, post-exploitation, and remediation reporting
Red team exercise — covert, objective-based adversary simulation targeting people, processes, and technology over an extended multi-week period
Bug bounty program — crowd-sourced researcher submissions rewarded by the target organization based on severity and proof-of-concept quality
questions.explanation: The scenario describes a standard penetration test: scoped, authorized reconnaissance; active exploitation of a discovered vulnerability; post-exploitation lateral movement; and a remediation report — the defining phases of a penetration testing engagement. A vulnerability assessment stops before active exploitation. A red team exercise is typically covert and objective-based rather than constrained to a specific service scope. A bug bounty is an ongoing crowd-sourced program, not a structured firm engagement with a defined statement of work.

questions.question: What is threat intelligence?
options: Automatically updated antivirus signature databases that security vendors push to endpoints hourly to detect newly identified malware variants and heuristic behavioral patterns from threat labs
Network performance telemetry collected from routers, switches, and WAN links to baseline utilization, detect saturation anomalies, and inform capacity planning and procurement decisions
Behavioral analytics generated from user workstation and server telemetry that detect deviations from established activity baselines and generate alerts for potential insider threat investigation
Curated information about existing and emerging threats including TTPs (tactics, techniques, procedures), IOCs, and threat actor profiles, used to improve defenses proactively
questions.explanation: Threat intelligence (TI) provides context about threats: who attacks, how they attack, what they target. Sources: OSINT, dark web, ISACs, commercial feeds. Feeds into SIEM, firewalls, and incident response.

questions.question: A retail company's POS terminals, corporate workstations, and internal file servers all share a flat Layer 2 network with no VLAN separation. After a POS malware incident, forensics shows the attacker pivoted directly from the infected terminal to the HR file server. Which architectural change would have MOST limited the attacker's ability to move laterally after the initial POS compromise?
options: Deploy a next-generation firewall at the internet edge to inspect and block inbound threats before they reach any host on the corporate LAN
Implement VLAN segmentation and inter-zone access controls to isolate POS terminals from HR servers and corporate workstations in separate network zones
Enable endpoint detection and response on all POS terminals to detect malware and automatically isolate infected hosts before lateral movement to adjacent systems can occur
Require 802.1X certificate-based port authentication on all switch ports to prevent unauthorized or rogue endpoints from joining any network segment without valid supplicant credentials
questions.explanation: Network segmentation with VLANs and inter-zone firewall rules contains lateral movement — a POS terminal in its own isolated zone cannot reach HR servers unless a rule explicitly permits that path. A perimeter firewall (option A) would not have helped here because both the initial compromise and the subsequent pivot occurred entirely on the internal network, after the attacker was already inside the perimeter.

questions.question: A hospital's security team is paged at 2 AM when clinical systems go offline due to ransomware. With patient data encrypted and operations impaired, team members are uncertain who leads containment, who notifies regulators, and what technical steps should follow. Which organizational document, prepared in advance, defines these roles and procedures and guides the team through the response?
options: Business Continuity Plan — describes how essential operations continue during any major disruption through alternate staffing and manual workarounds, independent of security-specific containment or forensics
Disaster Recovery Plan — documents the RTO and RPO targets and the technical steps for restoring IT infrastructure and data from backup after a catastrophic service failure
Incident Response Plan — predefines team roles, escalation contacts, containment steps, eradication tasks, and recovery procedures that activate the moment a security incident is declared
Risk Register — catalogs identified risks with likelihood and impact ratings and the treatment controls approved by governance leadership for each risk category
questions.explanation: An incident response plan provides the pre-practiced playbook for security events — who leads, who communicates with legal and regulators, and what technical steps occur in sequence, so no time is lost making decisions under pressure. A disaster recovery plan overlaps in the recovery phase but focuses on restoring IT infrastructure from backups rather than on the containment, eradication, and forensic procedures that define security incident response.

questions.question: What is the difference between IDS and IPS?
options: IDS and IPS are functionally identical — both sit inline on the network and actively block all suspicious traffic
IPS is software-only running on endpoints; IDS is always deployed as dedicated network appliance hardware
IDS: detects and alerts on suspicious activity (passive). IPS: detects AND actively blocks/drops malicious traffic (inline)
IDS blocks unknown traffic by default; IPS uses passive monitoring only and requires manual operator confirmation
questions.explanation: IDS (Intrusion Detection System) monitors and alerts — doesn't block. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System) sits inline and blocks malicious traffic in real time. Both use signatures and anomaly detection.

questions.question: What is steganography in security?
options: A symmetric block cipher that encrypts plaintext into ciphertext using a secret shared key and initialization vector
A firewall evasion technique that fragments large network packets into smaller units to bypass DPI signatures
A network traffic obfuscation method that tunnels C2 communications through encrypted DNS queries to evade defenses
The practice of hiding secret data within ordinary, non-secret files (images, audio, video) to avoid detection — the existence of the message is concealed
questions.explanation: Steganography hides messages within cover files. Example: embedding secret text in the least significant bits of image pixels. Different from encryption — encryption hides the content; steganography hides the existence.

questions.question: What is a supply chain attack?
options: Compromising software or hardware through a trusted third-party supplier or partner — e.g., injecting malicious code into software updates (SolarWinds, 3CX)
A physical intrusion against warehouse facilities to disrupt distribution of hardware components or product shipments
A volumetric denial-of-service campaign targeting an organization's e-commerce system during high-traffic retail periods
A spear phishing campaign targeting procurement staff to gain approval for fraudulent hardware purchase orders
questions.explanation: Supply chain attacks target trusted software vendors. Attackers compromise a legitimate software update or hardware component, affecting all downstream customers who trust and install it. Very difficult to detect.

questions.question: What is CVSS (Common Vulnerability Scoring System)?
options: A certificate authority validation standard that browsers use to determine whether an SSL/TLS issuer is globally trusted
A standardized framework for rating the severity of software vulnerabilities on a 0-10 scale — used to prioritize patching and remediation
A compliance scoring methodology under PCI DSS rating cardholder data environments across twelve control areas
An antivirus detection effectiveness benchmark measuring how many known malware samples a product identifies in labs
questions.explanation: CVSS v3 rates vulnerabilities 0-10: Critical (9-10), High (7-8.9), Medium (4-6.9), Low (0.1-3.9). Considers attack vector, complexity, privileges needed, user interaction, and impact to CIA.

questions.question: What is a pass-the-hash attack?
options: Transmitting a password hash to peers via a secure channel to enable shared service account authentication across systems
A hash collision technique that generates a second input matching a target hash to forge signatures on malicious documents
Using a captured NTLM password hash directly for authentication without knowing the plaintext password — allows lateral movement in Windows environments
A brute-force technique iterating through precomputed hash lists to identify weak credentials in a shadow password file
questions.explanation: In Windows, NTLM authentication sends the hash, not the password. An attacker who captures a hash can use it directly to authenticate. Mitigations: Credential Guard, LAPS, disable NTLM where possible.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a WAF (Web Application Firewall)?
options: A next-generation firewall at the network perimeter inspecting and controlling east-west and north-south IP traffic flows
An endpoint protection platform combining antivirus, EDR, and DLP to defend workstations against malware and exfiltration
A bandwidth management tool that monitors and shapes traffic to enforce QoS policies and prevent saturation
Inspects HTTP/HTTPS traffic and filters attacks targeting web applications — blocks SQL injection, XSS, CSRF, and OWASP Top 10 attacks
questions.explanation: WAF operates at Layer 7 analyzing HTTP request content. Can be deployed as hardware, software, or cloud service (AWS WAF, Cloudflare, ModSecurity). Uses signature and behavioral rules to block web attacks.

questions.question: A security analyst reviewing authentication logs observes thousands of failed login attempts against a single account over two hours. Each attempt uses a different password following an alphabetical sequence: 'aaaa', 'aaab', 'aaac'. No leaked credential data was involved, and account lockout was disabled by a misconfiguration. Which attack type BEST describes this pattern?
options: Password spraying — tests one commonly used password across many different accounts to stay under per-account lockout thresholds, trading depth per account for breadth across the user population
Credential stuffing — replays known username-password pairs from a publicly leaked breach database against the target, relying on password reuse across services rather than generated strings
Dictionary attack — iterates through a curated wordlist of likely passwords and phrases rather than exhaustively testing every possible sequential character combination from scratch
Brute force attack — tests every possible character combination in sequence until the correct credential is found, without relying on wordlists or prior breach data
questions.explanation: The alphabetical sequential pattern ('aaaa', 'aaab'...) is the defining characteristic of brute force — it tests every combination without any prior knowledge of which passwords are likely. A dictionary attack would show wordlist entries like 'password123'; credential stuffing would use real email-password pairs from a breach; password spraying would target many accounts with one common password rather than exhausting all combinations against a single account.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a PKI certificate chain of trust?
options: Encrypts all network sessions between clients and servers by establishing TLS connections using the server's public certificate to negotiate a symmetric session key and authenticate the connection
Establishes trusted certificate authorities through a hierarchy: Root CA → Intermediate CA → End-entity certificate. Browsers trust root CAs; all certs signed by trusted CAs are automatically trusted
Provides network access control by validating 802.1X supplicant certificates against an internal RADIUS server before permitting devices to join the corporate LAN or wireless network segment
Defines firewall policy rules based on certificate subject names, permitting traffic only when both source and destination endpoints present valid end-entity certs signed by the enterprise CA
questions.explanation: PKI chain: Root CA (self-signed, offline, highly protected) signs Intermediate CA, which signs end-entity certs (web servers, users). Browsers/OSes have built-in trusted root CA stores. Revoke an intermediate to invalidate all its children.

questions.question: What is DNSSEC?
options: A firewall module that filters DNS queries by reputation, blocking resolution of malicious or newly registered domains
A protocol tunneling DNS queries inside HTTPS connections to encrypt lookups and prevent ISP traffic analysis
DNS Security — adds authentication to DNS responses using digital signatures to prevent DNS cache poisoning
A DNS load balancing solution distributing queries across multiple authoritative nameservers via weighted round-robin
questions.explanation: DNSSEC uses digital signatures (public key cryptography) to authenticate DNS records. Prevents cache poisoning/spoofing attacks where an attacker redirects users to malicious servers by injecting fake DNS responses.

questions.question: What is a rootkit?
options: A legitimate system administration toolkit granting elevated privileges to IT staff for remote server management
An antivirus scanning engine running at the kernel level to detect and terminate malicious processes before memory access
A network vulnerability scanner that identifies hosts running as root and reports privilege escalation risks for auditing
Malware designed to gain root/admin access and hide itself and other malicious processes from the OS and security tools — extremely difficult to detect and remove
questions.explanation: Rootkits modify the OS kernel or firmware to hide malicious activity. Kernel rootkits intercept system calls. Bootkit rootkits persist in MBR/UEFI. Detection requires out-of-band scanning (offline boot media) or firmware re-flash.

questions.question: What is the principle of 'need to know' in security?
options: Users should only have access to information required to perform their specific job function — even if they have clearance for higher classifications
All employees within a department should share equal access to the same data repositories regardless of individual roles
Users with appropriate security clearance automatically gain access to all information at or below that classification level
Managers should be able to access all data their direct reports can view in order to maintain oversight and compliance
questions.explanation: 'Need to know' restricts access even among users with appropriate clearance levels. A classified user only gets access to specific classified information relevant to their role — not all classified data.

questions.question: What is a security token (hardware token)?
options: A software password manager installed on mobile devices that auto-fills stored credentials in browser login forms
A physical device generating time-based one-time passwords (TOTP) for MFA — examples: RSA SecurID, YubiKey, hardware OTP tokens
A proximity badge using RFID to authenticate employees at physical access control points such as server room doors
A smart card device that stores static credentials and requires insertion into a card reader on the user's workstation
questions.explanation: Hardware tokens provide 'something you have' MFA factor. TOTP tokens (HMAC-based time synchronization) generate 6-8 digit codes every 30 seconds. FIDO2/WebAuthn tokens (YubiKey) provide phishing-resistant authentication.

questions.question: What is credential harvesting?
options: A privileged access management practice that rotates service account passwords on a schedule and vaults credentials in PAM
A secure password reset workflow requiring users to verify identity through email OTP before updating their credentials
An attack technique collecting large numbers of credentials through phishing, data breaches, keyloggers, or man-in-the-middle attacks for use in credential stuffing
An identity governance process that periodically reviews user entitlements to ensure access aligns with current job roles
questions.explanation: Credential harvesting gathers username/password pairs at scale via fake login pages (phishing), compromising databases, keyloggers, or traffic interception. Harvested credentials used for account takeover and lateral movement.

questions.question: A tier-1 SOC analyst handles 80 identical low-severity alerts each shift: look up the source IP against a threat feed, add an enforcement rule to the firewall if malicious, then close the ticket. The SOC manager wants to automate this repetitive workflow entirely so analysts can focus on complex investigations requiring human judgment. Which technology is purpose-built for this use case?
options: SIEM — ingests and correlates log data from firewalls, endpoints, and servers across the environment to surface prioritized threat alerts for analyst investigation and retrospective threat hunting
EDR — continuously records endpoint process creation, file modifications, and network connections, applying behavioral analytics to detect threats that bypass traditional signature-based defenses
SOAR — executes automated playbooks that enrich incoming alerts, coordinate response actions across integrated security tools, and resolve routine tickets without requiring analyst intervention
XDR — correlates detection telemetry across endpoints, network, cloud, and identity into a unified platform that surfaces multi-vector attack patterns invisible to individual siloed security tools
questions.explanation: SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) is purpose-built to automate repetitive, well-defined alert workflows using scripted playbooks — exactly the enrich-block-close pattern the analyst performs manually each shift. A SIEM surfaces alerts but does not act on them; it feeds SOAR rather than replacing it. EDR and XDR extend detection coverage but neither automates ticket-handling playbooks for routine low-severity alert triage.

questions.question: A company hires a penetration tester after an employee fell for a phishing email that delivered an initial access payload. The client wants to simulate the attacker's position from that point forward. The tester is given only a standard employee's Active Directory credentials and a VPN profile — no system diagrams, no source code, no admin access. Which engagement type matches this scope?
options: Black-box — the tester starts with no credentials and no prior information, replicating an unaided external attacker scanning from the internet
White-box — the tester receives full architecture documentation, source code, and elevated credentials to achieve maximum assessment depth
Gray-box — the tester holds a standard user account and no architecture documentation, matching the attacker's post-phish foothold
Red team — a multi-phase exercise spanning several weeks that combines OSINT, social engineering, lateral movement, and physical intrusion attempts
questions.explanation: Gray-box testing gives the tester limited but realistic access — in this case a standard employee account — to simulate a threat actor who has completed initial access via phishing but lacks insider knowledge of the architecture. Black-box testing would not match because the attacker already has credentials; white-box would provide far greater access (admin, source code) than the scenario describes.

questions.question: An employee installs a free screen-recording utility downloaded from a third-party website. The recording features work correctly, but the company's EDR detects the application quietly exfiltrating documents to an external server in the background. No separate malware process was installed — the behavior originates entirely from within the user-installed application. Which malware category BEST describes this threat?
options: Ransomware — malware that encrypts the victim's files and withholds decryption until the victim pays a ransom, typically in cryptocurrency
Worm — self-replicating malware that propagates autonomously to adjacent hosts by exploiting vulnerabilities or abusing shared file systems
Trojan — malicious code embedded within an otherwise functional application that activates its hidden payload when the user runs it
Rootkit — kernel-level or firmware malware designed to conceal its presence and other malicious processes from host security controls
questions.explanation: A Trojan conceals malicious functionality within an application that appears legitimate or useful — the victim installs and runs it willingly, triggering the hidden payload. Unlike a worm, a Trojan does not self-propagate to other hosts. Unlike ransomware, it does not encrypt files for extortion. Unlike a rootkit, it does not subvert kernel structures to hide itself from the OS. The screen-recording utility that silently exfiltrates data while appearing functional is the textbook Trojan scenario.

questions.question: What is the purpose of network segmentation and microsegmentation?
options: Aggregates multiple physical network links into a single logical bonded interface to improve available throughput and provide link redundancy between core distribution switches and server racks
Reduces hardware procurement and total operational costs by virtualizing routing, switching, and firewall functions onto a smaller number of physical chassis within the data center environment
Divides networks into isolated zones (segmentation) or workload-level isolation (microsegmentation) to limit lateral movement after a breach — zero trust principle
Simplifies network management by reducing the total number of routing domains and eliminating subnet boundaries to create a flatter, unified architecture that is easier to operate at scale
questions.explanation: Network segmentation: VLANs, firewalls between zones. Microsegmentation (software-defined): granular per-workload policies (e.g., VMware NSX, Cisco ACI). Both limit blast radius if an attacker compromises one zone.

questions.question: What is a birthday attack in cryptography?
options: A targeted phishing campaign sent to employees exploiting personal events to capture credentials through a fake HR form
A timing side-channel attack measuring cryptographic operation durations to infer private key bits statistically
An annual security test where organizations validate all encryption implementations against newly discovered vulnerabilities
Exploits the birthday paradox probability to find hash collisions — two different inputs producing the same hash value — weakening hash function integrity
questions.explanation: The birthday paradox: the probability of two people sharing a birthday reaches 50% at just 23 people. Similarly, hash collisions are found much faster than expected. MD5 is broken; SHA-256 provides much higher collision resistance.

questions.question: What is a man-in-the-browser attack?
options: Malware infects the browser itself, intercepting and modifying transactions in real-time — even HTTPS provides no protection since the attack is inside the encrypted session
A hardware keylogger placed between the keyboard and computer to capture credentials without leaving software forensic traces
An attack targeting browser extension repositories to publish malicious add-ons that steal saved passwords and session cookies
A SQL injection attack delivered through a browser-based application targeting a backend database with user credential data
questions.explanation: MITB attacks (e.g., ZeuS, SpyEye) infect the browser via malicious extensions or process injection. They intercept banking transactions after the user authenticates, modifying payee/amount before submission.

questions.question: What is access control best described as?
options: Physical building security controls including badge readers, biometric mantraps, and CCTV systems that restrict and monitor entry to facilities by authorized personnel and contractors
Mechanisms controlling who can access resources and what operations they can perform — implemented through identification, authentication, authorization, and accountability
Network firewall rule sets that control packet flow by permitting or blocking traffic based on source and destination IP addresses, port numbers, and protocol state information
Password complexity requirements, expiration schedules, and lockout policies enforced across domain accounts to ensure credentials meet minimum strength and rotation standards
questions.explanation: Access control encompasses all mechanisms for controlling resource access: physical (locks, badges), logical (passwords, MFA, RBAC), administrative (policies, procedures). Security models: DAC, MAC, RBAC, ABAC.

questions.question: What is a logic bomb?
options: A physical device planted inside server hardware by a disgruntled employee to destroy equipment on a specific date, timed to activate after the insider's departure from the organization
Ransomware that immediately and indiscriminately encrypts all reachable drives upon first execution, without requiring any external condition or network connectivity to trigger the payload
Malicious code that executes when specific conditions are met — e.g., a disgruntled employee's code that deletes files on a future date or if their account is disabled
An automated port scanning utility scheduled to run reconnaissance sweeps during overnight maintenance windows specifically to avoid triggering daytime intrusion detection monitoring systems
questions.explanation: Logic bombs lie dormant until triggered by conditions (date, time, specific action, file existence). Typically planted by insiders. Prevention: code reviews, separation of duties, monitoring for unusual scheduled tasks.

questions.question: What is the purpose of input validation in application security?
options: Compressing submitted form data on the client side before transmission to reduce total bandwidth consumption, lower server processing overhead, and improve page rendering speed for end users
Encrypting all data received from users in transit using TLS 1.3 with forward-secrecy cipher suites to prevent interception of sensitive form submissions by network-layer eavesdroppers
Logging all user input interactions with web application forms into a tamper-proof audit trail for regulatory compliance reporting and subsequent digital forensic investigation
Ensuring user input meets expected format, type, and range requirements before processing — prevents injection attacks (SQL, XSS, command injection, buffer overflow)
questions.explanation: Input validation + sanitization is the primary defense against injection attacks. Validate on server side (never trust client-side only). Use parameterized queries for SQL, encode output for XSS, restrict file uploads by type/size.

questions.question: What is non-repudiation in information security?
options: The ability to prove that a specific action was taken by a specific entity — preventing them from denying it. Achieved through digital signatures, audit logs, and timestamps
An organizational policy of refusing to publicly disclose a security breach until legal counsel has assessed liability and approved the content of all external communications
A data retention requirement archiving encrypted communications for a minimum of seven years to satisfy financial, healthcare, and government regulatory compliance obligations
An incident response obligation formally notifying affected individuals and regulators that a breach occurred within the mandatory timeframe under applicable data protection legislation
questions.explanation: Non-repudiation ensures that parties cannot deny their actions. Digital signatures provide non-repudiation (only the private key owner could sign). Audit logs with integrity protection provide non-repudiation for system actions.

questions.question: What is a zero trust security model?
options: A perimeter-centric security model applying rigorous identity controls at the corporate network edge while granting implicit trust to all traffic from authenticated users on the internal LAN segment

'Never trust, always verify' — requires strict identity verification for every user and device regardless of network location. Assumes breach and minimizes blast radius with least privilege and microsegmentation
A certificate-based model granting access to any device presenting a certificate from an organization-approved CA, without separately evaluating user identity, device posture, or behavioral context
A zero-tolerance compliance framework requiring strict disciplinary enforcement against employees who violate acceptable use policies, with no exceptions extended to executives or privileged accounts
questions.explanation: Zero Trust principles: verify explicitly (always authenticate/authorize with all available signals), use least privilege access, assume breach (design for containment, limit lateral movement). Contrasts with perimeter-based 'trust inside the network'.

questions.question: What is the purpose of a CISO?
options: A technical security analytics platform correlating alerts across endpoint, network, cloud, and email telemetry to produce a unified operational risk dashboard and prioritized investigation queue
A vendor-neutral professional certification program validating engineers' hands-on configuration knowledge across firewall policy management, IDS signature tuning, and SIEM query development
Chief Information Security Officer — executive responsible for an organization's information security strategy, risk management, compliance, and security team leadership
A NIST regulatory compliance framework organizations adopt to achieve FedRAMP or FISMA authorization and demonstrate adequate cybersecurity controls to federal oversight bodies
questions.explanation: The CISO bridges technical security and business leadership. Responsible for: security strategy and roadmap, risk management, compliance (SOC 2, ISO 27001), incident response oversight, security awareness, and board reporting.

questions.question: What is the purpose of code signing?
options: Encrypts application source code repositories so developers must authenticate with a signing certificate before committing
A peer code review process where engineers inspect each other's changes for logic errors and security flaws before merge
An access control mechanism restricting which developers can modify specific modules based on their team role and seniority
Uses digital signatures to verify software authenticity and integrity — proves the software came from a known publisher and hasn't been tampered with since signing
questions.explanation: Code signing uses a publisher's private key to sign executables. The OS verifies the signature against the publisher's certificate. If tampered, the signature breaks. Prevents malicious code injection into legitimate software.

questions.question: What is a PKI (Public Key Infrastructure)?
options: A framework of CAs, certificates, keys, and policies enabling trusted cryptographic communication — components: Root CA, Subordinate CA, certificate templates, CRL, OCSP responder
A physical key management system storing master encryption keys inside locked tamper-evident cabinets requiring dual custodian authorization before any key retrieval or duplication operation
A privileged access management solution generating random credentials for service accounts and storing them in an encrypted vault with automatic rotation on a configurable schedule
A network firewall rule framework defining which source IP subnets may communicate with destination segments using encrypted channels through the perimeter security appliance
questions.explanation: PKI: Root CA (trust anchor, offline), Subordinate/Issuing CAs (online, issue end-entity certs), Registration Authority, certificate store, revocation (CRL/OCSP). Basis for TLS, code signing, smart card auth, S/MIME email encryption.

questions.question: What is stealth/evasion techniques used by attackers?
options: Physical camouflage methods and social pretexting scripts used by red team operators to blend into office environments and assess physical security controls during authorized penetration engagements
Anti-forensics, encoding/obfuscation (base64, hex), timestomping (modifying file timestamps), log clearing, living off the land (using built-in OS tools), fragmented packets to bypass IDS signatures
Network packet compression algorithms reducing transmission overhead to improve bandwidth efficiency and lower latency costs across enterprise WAN, MPLS, and SD-WAN circuit deployments
DDoS mitigation strategies including traffic scrubbing, anycast routing, BGP blackholing, and rate limiting used by defenders to neutralize volumetric and protocol-level attack traffic
questions.explanation: Attackers evade detection by: using LOLBins (PowerShell, WMI), encoding payloads, clearing event logs, altering timestamps, fragmenting traffic to bypass IDS. Defense: behavioral detection (EDR), log integrity (SIEM with immutable logs).

questions.question: What is a security audit vs a security assessment?
options: Security audit and security assessment are interchangeable terms for the same engagement; both are conducted internally by the security team without reference to any external compliance standard or framework

Security audits find technical vulnerabilities by actively probing live systems with exploitation tools; security assessments are purely passive document reviews comparing written policy to industry best practices

Security audit: formal review against a standard (ISO 27001, NIST CSF, PCI DSS) — compliance-focused, produces pass/fail. Security assessment: broader evaluation of security posture, risks, and controls — not necessarily compliance-tied
Security assessments are consistently cheaper than audits because fewer auditors are required; security audits rely entirely on automated tooling and require minimal hands-on assessor involvement
questions.explanation: Audit: checks compliance against defined controls/standards, formal opinion (pass/qualified). Assessment: risk-based evaluation of overall security posture. Organizations need both: audits for compliance, assessments for risk management.

questions.question: What is a rainbow table attack?
options: A network attack that poisons ARP caches using crafted gratuitous packets to redirect LAN traffic through an attacker-controlled host, enabling credential theft and man-in-the-middle interception
A power side-channel attack that measures variations in device power consumption during cryptographic operations to statistically infer individual private key bits without direct memory access
A large-scale credential stuffing campaign that systematically cycles username and password combinations sourced from publicly leaked breach databases against target authentication endpoints
Precomputed table of hashes mapped to plaintexts — enables fast password recovery by looking up a hash in the table. Defeated by salting (adding random value to each password before hashing)
questions.explanation: Rainbow tables precompute hash(password) for millions of passwords — lookup is instant. Defense: salting adds a random value per user before hashing (stored with the hash). Even with table, attacker must rebuild one for each salt. Modern algorithms: bcrypt, Argon2, scrypt all include salt automatically.

questions.question: What is an incident response chain of custody?
options: Documentation tracking the collection, handling, and transfer of digital evidence — ensures evidence integrity and admissibility in legal proceedings by establishing a clear, unbroken record
A user activity monitoring log that records all file system accesses, authentication events, and outbound network connections for use in compliance audit reviews and regulatory reporting
An automated ITSM workflow that tracks the full lifecycle of security alerts from initial triage through analyst assignment, investigation, and final resolution closure by the SOC team
A patch management database documenting vulnerability identification, testing results, change approval, production deployment, and rollback procedures for every system update applied
questions.explanation: Chain of custody documents: who collected evidence, when, where, how, storage conditions, and every person who had access. Hash values verify integrity. Breaks in chain of custody can make evidence inadmissible in court.

questions.question: What is OAuth 2.0 and how is it used?
options: A password hashing standard that applies PBKDF2 with a random salt to user credentials before storage, protecting the hash database from precomputed rainbow table and brute-force attacks
An authorization framework enabling third-party applications to obtain limited access to user accounts on an HTTP service without exposing the user's credentials — e.g., 'Log in with Google'
A federated authentication protocol using XML-based security assertions to enable SSO between enterprise identity providers and cloud-hosted service providers in B2B integration scenarios
A network encryption protocol securing service-to-service API communications within a Kubernetes cluster using mutual TLS certificates issued by an internal certificate authority
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0: authorization delegation. 'Log in with Google' gives an app an access token (scoped permissions) — the app never sees your Google password. OIDC (OpenID Connect) adds authentication on top of OAuth 2.0.

questions.question: What is a Security Operations Center (SOC)?
options: A physically secured server room housing network and compute equipment, protected by biometric entry, mantrap access control, CCTV surveillance, and environmental monitoring systems
A physical security team responsible for guard patrols, visitor access management, proximity badge issuance, and perimeter surveillance monitoring at all corporate facilities and campuses
A centralized team responsible for monitoring, detecting, investigating, and responding to security incidents 24/7 — uses SIEM, threat intelligence, and orchestration tools (SOAR)
A regulatory compliance department reviewing internal audit findings, tracking remediation milestone timelines, and reporting control status and exception management to executive leadership
questions.explanation: SOC Tier 1: alert triage/monitoring. Tier 2: investigation and analysis. Tier 3: threat hunting and advanced analysis. Tools: SIEM (detect), SOAR (automate responses), EDR (endpoint visibility), threat intelligence feeds.

questions.question: What is a DKIM/SPF/DMARC email security framework?
options: End-to-end email content encryption using S/MIME certificates or PGP key pairs to encrypt the message body so only the intended recipient holding the corresponding private key can decrypt it
Email gateway virus scanning protocols that inspect every inbound attachment and embedded URL against up-to-date threat intelligence feeds to identify and quarantine malicious messages
A cloud email proxy protocol routing all inbound and outbound messages through a managed filtering service to apply content policies, perform archiving, and enforce compliance retention rules

SPF: DNS record listing authorized mail servers. DKIM: cryptographic signature on emails proving sending server. DMARC: policy specifying what to do with SPF/DKIM failures (none/quarantine/reject) — together prevent email spoofing
questions.explanation: Email authentication trio: SPF (which IPs can send for domain), DKIM (signature proving message integrity), DMARC (policy: if SPF and DKIM both fail, quarantine or reject). Essential for preventing phishing via domain impersonation.

questions.question: What is application allowlisting (whitelisting)?
options: Only pre-approved, explicitly listed applications are permitted to run — all others are blocked by default. Most effective defense against malware but high administrative overhead
A security posture where all executable applications run by default unless they match a known-bad signature in the vendor-managed threat intelligence block list database
A firewall rule strategy blocking specific known-malicious IP addresses and domain names at the perimeter while permitting outbound connections to all other internet destinations by default
An MDM policy restricting application store category access rather than controlling individual application identities, applied to corporate-managed mobile devices in BYOD environments
questions.explanation: Application allowlisting (Windows Defender Application Control/AppLocker, Carbon Black) is the most secure endpoint posture — only known-good apps execute. Opposite of traditional AV (blocklist). Very effective against zero-days and fileless attacks.

questions.question: What is a hardware security module (HSM)?
options: A USB-connected portable storage device with hardware AES-128 encryption and PIN-protection, designed for secure file transport between air-gapped or classified computing environments

A dedicated hardware device that performs cryptographic operations and securely stores keys — tamper-resistant, cannot export private keys. Used for PKI root CAs, HSMs in cloud (AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM)
A software cryptographic module embedded in the operating system kernel that manages TLS session key generation for web servers using software-protected key storage without hardware isolation
A rack-mounted network security appliance integrating stateful firewall, intrusion detection, and VPN termination into a single hardened platform deployed at the enterprise perimeter
questions.explanation: HSMs provide: hardware-backed key storage (keys never leave the HSM in plaintext), certified cryptographic operations, tamper evidence/protection. Required for PCI DSS (payment HSMs), banking, and PKI root CAs. FIPS 140-2 Level 3+ certified.

questions.question: What is a spear phishing attack?
options: A mass phishing campaign sent simultaneously to millions of unrelated recipients using generic lures such as shipping notifications or banking alerts, without any personalization of the content
A vishing attack conducted by telephone in which an attacker impersonates IT support staff or a bank fraud department to pressure victims into verbally disclosing credentials or OTP codes

A targeted phishing attack customized for a specific individual or organization — uses personal details (name, role, colleagues, recent events) to appear highly convincing. Often the entry point for APT attacks
A USB drop attack where adversaries plant infected removable drives in parking lots and lobbies, relying on employee curiosity to inadvertently introduce malware into the corporate environment
questions.explanation: Spear phishing success rate >> mass phishing because it's personalized. Attacker researches target on LinkedIn, company website, social media. Then crafts an email from 'their CEO' or 'IT helpdesk' about something plausible. High-value targets: executives, finance, IT admins.

questions.question: What is a CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker)?
options: A cloud-native firewall service that filters inbound and outbound VPC traffic at the network layer based on security group rules, ACLs, and route table policies defined per cloud account
A cloud identity provider federating on-premises Active Directory credentials with cloud-hosted SaaS applications via SAML 2.0 assertions or OIDC tokens for SSO access management
An API gateway service that validates JWT authentication tokens, enforces per-client rate limits, and routes API requests between consumers and backend microservices in a cloud platform

A security policy enforcement point between cloud service consumers and providers — provides visibility into shadow IT, enforces DLP, detects anomalous behavior, and controls data movement to cloud services
questions.explanation: CASBs (Netskope, McAfee MVISION, Microsoft CASB) discover what cloud apps employees use (shadow IT), enforce policies (block sensitive data uploads to personal Dropbox), detect risky behavior, and provide compliance controls for cloud usage.

questions.question: What is endpoint detection and response (EDR)?
options: Continuous monitoring and collection of endpoint data with automated analysis to detect threats that bypass traditional AV — provides investigation capabilities and automated/manual response (isolate, kill process)
Traditional antivirus software that scans executable files against a local signature database at scheduled intervals, quarantining any file matching a known malware hash or pattern
A network intrusion detection system that captures and inspects packet payloads in transit, matching content against known attack signatures and logging events to a central SIEM platform
A centralized log management platform that aggregates raw events from endpoints, servers, and network devices and stores them for search and manual analysis by security engineers
questions.explanation: EDR (CrowdStrike Falcon, SentinelOne, Microsoft Defender for Endpoint) records all endpoint activity (process creation, network connections, file changes), uses ML/behavioral analysis to detect threats, and enables forensic investigation.

questions.question: What is a cryptographic hash function and what properties must it have?
options: A reversible symmetric encryption function that accepts variable-length plaintext along with a secret key to produce ciphertext of the same length, suitable for subsequent decryption and recovery

A one-way function producing fixed-length output. Required properties: deterministic, one-way (can't reverse), collision-resistant (different inputs → different outputs), avalanche effect (small input change → completely different output)
A symmetric block cipher operating in CBC or GCM mode to encrypt data at rest, producing output of a length equivalent to the original input rounded up to the nearest cipher block boundary
A key exchange protocol that enables two parties to independently derive an identical shared secret value across an untrusted public channel without ever directly transmitting the secret
questions.explanation: Hash functions (SHA-256, SHA-3, MD5 [broken]): file integrity checking, password storage, digital signatures, blockchain. MD5 and SHA-1 are broken (collision attacks demonstrated). Use SHA-256 or SHA-3 for security-sensitive applications.

questions.question: What is defense in depth?
options: A deep packet inspection technique that fully reassembles TCP byte streams before inspecting application-layer payloads for attack signatures and protocol anomalies on stateful network appliances
A perimeter-centric firewall configuration methodology placing all security controls at the network edge, extending implicit trust to internal traffic once it crosses the boundary

A security strategy using multiple overlapping security controls in layers — if one layer fails, others prevent compromise. Layers: physical, network, host, application, data, user. No single point of failure
An architectural model relying on a single high-throughput next-generation firewall to inspect, filter, and log all traffic entering and leaving the corporate network simultaneously
questions.explanation: Defense in depth (Swiss cheese model): multiple imperfect controls whose holes don't overlap. Examples: perimeter firewall + network segmentation + host firewall + EDR + SIEM + user training. Attacker must defeat multiple controls.

questions.question: What is the principle of fail-safe defaults in security?
options: Systems should fail open and maintain service availability when errors occur, prioritizing uptime over strict access control
Systems should continue operating in a degraded mode during partial failures to preserve as much user functionality as possible
A disaster recovery principle ensuring backup systems take over automatically within defined RTO and RPO thresholds
By default, access should be denied unless explicitly granted — systems should fail to a secure (closed) state when errors occur, not to an open/permissive state
